value.summary: The conservatory's public receiving rooms were established after the Marriage of the Two Harbours as Serevan carriers borrowed useful signal and inspection practices from Veymouth and Nacre Quay. It was not a royal wedding palace, and the western harbours did not acquire sovereignty here. Silting, subsidence and repeated rebuilding gradually put the lower rooms underwater. Today ferryperson Liora Senn carries schoolchildren beside traders, charging by a posted fare rather than the grandeur of their ancestors' portraits. Historical threads: The Marriage of the Two Harbours; The Address Beneath the Blue Paint.
value.provenance: Nine Wonders of Caldris; reconciled with the existing chronology before campaign play.

value.summary: Before a boat is lowered, the newest worker reads the stop signal and the oldest worker demonstrates that it still works. Hulls carry names of lost vessels, but the crew maintains a list distinguishing memorial names from original timbers. Visitors buy lunch at the cooperative table; paying for a tour does not authorise entry to a suspended work cradle.
value.provenance: Nine Wonders of Caldris; reconciled with the existing chronology before campaign play.

value.summary: The chain was substituted by a supplier trying to keep an underpaid workshop solvent, not by a foreign saboteur. The material is unsafe for the heaviest cradle. Records hidden in a patched rib also show that the cooperative once accepted a profitable priority repair that delayed a poorer community's boat. The lower loading gear can be shut without cutting off the inspected upper-yard path.
value.provenance: Nine Wonders of Caldris; reconciled with the existing chronology before campaign play.

value.summary: A valuable keel has been pledged to two creditors who each claim the next repaired ship. A replacement chain arrives with excellent paperwork and the wrong iron. An apprentice finds a refuge account inside a reused hull, complicating a celebrated story about which merchants kept people fed during the sailing shortage.
value.provenance: Nine Wonders of Caldris; reconciled with the existing chronology before campaign play.

value.summary: The upper works were expanded during the Salt Without Sails disruptions, when inland and coastal shortages made repairing smaller craft more useful than waiting for a great fleet. Later generations replaced most of the original timber. Recent arguments at Gullstrand's Closed Launch revived the harbour workers' older right to refuse an unsafe lowering, making this an important witness site for the history of practical judgement and maritime labour. Historical threads: Salt Without Sails; The Hearing at the Closed Launch.
value.provenance: Nine Wonders of Caldris; reconciled with the existing chronology before campaign play.

value.summary: A visitor may hang one lantern for someone who helped them, but the keeper lends the lantern rather than selling ownership of a rib. The last bowl of stew goes to whoever has arrived most recently. Climbing the head is forbidden during lambing, and the deep crawlspaces beneath the spring are outside the open shelter.
value.provenance: Nine Wonders of Caldris; reconciled with the existing chronology before campaign play.

value.summary: The strange lantern was hung by a frightened descendant using an old family name, not by a power predicting death. Beneath the spring is a reused grain chamber containing evidence that several respectable households charged for shelter during a later famine. The chamber is structurally unsafe and has no registered open approach. The stone figure itself neither wakes nor grants wishes.
value.provenance: Nine Wonders of Caldris; reconciled with the existing chronology before campaign play.

value.summary: A wealthy family offers to restore the cracked left hand if the communal hearth becomes its private memorial. A lantern bearing the name of a living traveller appears in a row usually used for the dead. Tessa needs someone to recover her first repair sketch from Highmead; without it, a well-meant new brace may obstruct the spring.
value.provenance: Nine Wonders of Caldris; reconciled with the existing chronology before campaign play.

value.summary: The colossus belongs to the same chalk country as the Button Hills granaries. People connect its open hearths with the Winter of Borrowed Hearths, but no surviving account proves that Maelin Rusk herself came here. A bowl is still set out for an absent guest. The dwarf mason Tessa Flintrill has returned every eleventh spring for almost a century; she recognises several families by their repaired cooking pots before she recognises their faces. Historical threads: The Winter of Borrowed Hearths; The War of False Weights.
value.provenance: Nine Wonders of Caldris; reconciled with the existing chronology before campaign play.
